# Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta (MN 142 (PTS MN iii 253))

**ID:** MN 142 (PTS MN iii 253)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Analysis of Religious Donations
**PTS:** MN iii 253
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta* ("The Exposition of Offerings" or "The Analysis of Religious Donations") is the 142nd discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, situated within the *Vibhaṅgavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Strauch 2014]. The discourse opens when the Buddha's foster mother, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, offers him a new robe that she had personally spun and woven; the Buddha declines to accept it as a personal gift and encourages her to offer it to the monastic Saṅgha instead [Anālayo 2016a]. Although Ānanda intervenes on her behalf by recalling her maternal care and devotion, the Buddha maintains that communal gifts to the Saṅgha yield far greater spiritual fruits than personal offerings [Anālayo 2011; Ohnuma 2006]. The Buddha then details fourteen classes of personal gifts (*pāṭipuggalikā dakkhiṇā*), seven grades of gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha—extending even to donations given on behalf of the Saṅgha to corrupt monks in a degenerate future age who wear ochre robes only around their necks (*kāsāvakantha*)—and the four ways an offering is purified by the virtue and intentions of the giver and receiver [Boucher 2008; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Ohnuma 2006].

Doctrinally, the discourse lists individuals practicing for the attainment of the four noble paths alongside those established in their fruition as distinct recipients of offerings [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2014]. This presents a notable tension with later Theravāda Abhidhamma and commentarial doctrine, which define the path as a single mind-moment directly followed by fruition; the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* harmonizes this by positing that a recipient attains the path at the very moment of receiving the gift [Anālayo 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016b].

- Passage-level parallels: AN 4.78 Dakkhiṇasutta

**Sources**

- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Dawn of Abhidharma (2014) — Analysis of the four path-attainers as recipients and the commentarial single-mind-moment interpretation.
- [Anālayo 2011] Bhikkhu Anālayo, 'Mahāpajāpatī’s Going Forth in the Madhyama-āgama' (2011) — Discussion of Ānanda's intervention regarding Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī's maternal role.
- [Boucher 2008] Daniel Boucher, Bodhisattvas of the Forest and the Formation of the Mahayana (2008) — Details on offerings to degenerate future monks with ochre necks (kāsāvakantha).
- [Anālayo 2016a] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Foundation History of the Nuns’ Order (2016) — Details on Mahāpajāpatī's robe-offering, spinning/weaving the cloth, and overview of parallels.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — English title, categorization under Vibhaṅgavagga, 14 personal and 7 Saṅgha offerings, and path-versus-fruition recipient tension.
- [Anālayo 2016b] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfully Facing Disease and Death (2016) — Description of the eight persons / four pairs as gift recipients and commentarial rationalization.
- [Ohnuma 2006] Reiko Ohnuma, 'Debt to the Mother' (2006) — Detailed analysis of the debt to the mother and the classification of gifts and merit.
- [Ohnuma 2012] Reiko Ohnuma, Ties That Bind: Maternal Imagery and Discourse in Indian Buddhism (2012) — Analysis of the opening section and maternal debt theme in MN 142.
- [Strauch 2007] Ingo Strauch, 'The Bajaur collection: A new collection of Kharoṣṭhī manuscripts' (2007) — Identification of the Gāndhārī fragment 1 of the Bajaur collection with MN 142 and comparison with MĀ 180.
- [Strauch 2014] Ingo Strauch in Alice Collett (ed.), Women in Early Indian Buddhism (2014) — Study of the Gāndhārī *Dhakṣiṇavibhaṅgasūtra, Chinese MĀ 180 (Gautamīsūtra), and Vibhaṅgavagga placement.
